title: Sharing the merit
hookLine: ending practice by dedicating whatever good was done to all beings
last: CANDLE AND INCENSE — LIGHT AND SCENT.

lines: POURED AT THE FOOT OF A TREE.
cards: At the end of a Buddhist ceremony in Thailand, something small happens that visitors often miss. While the monks chant, people pour water from a little vessel into a bowl, a thin, steady stream, until the chant ends.
Some hold a finger under the stream. Afterward, the water is often poured out at the foot of a tree. It looks like cleaning up.
It isn't. It's the last and, many Buddhists would say, one of the most beautiful parts of practice: giving away the good you've just done.

teach.h: PUNNA: THE GOOD FROM GOOD ACTIONS.
teach.b: The Pali word is punna, usually translated merit: the goodness that comes from good actions, like giving, keeping the precepts, meditating. You'd think the natural thing is to keep it.
But Buddhists across traditions end practice by sharing it. In Theravada this is called pattidana, the giving of merit. Its oldest roots are in a short text, the discourse outside the walls.
It pictures dead relatives waiting outside the walls of their old home, hoping someone will remember them.

When the living give food to monks and dedicate the gift, the text says the relatives can rejoice in it and be helped. The line people still chant is idam vo natinam hotu: may this be for our relatives.

That's what the water pouring is, and many chants that go with it compare the merit to rivers filling the ocean. Someone who hears of your good deed and says sadhu, well done, shares it too, by rejoicing.
In Mahayana traditions the dedication goes wider: at the end of a sitting or a chant, practitioners dedicate the merit to the awakening of all beings, everywhere, without exception.
Yesterday's candle comes back here, because teachers often explain the logic with one.
Light another candle from yours, and your flame doesn't get smaller. The room just gets brighter.
Merit shared isn't merit lost. It quietly changes the one who shares, too. Ending with a dedication keeps practice from becoming a private savings account.
You sat, you gave, you kept a precept, and then you open your hands again.

how: Buddhists across traditions end ceremonies and meditation by dedicating the merit to others; in Theravada countries this is often done by pouring water while monks chant, and in Mahayana traditions with a dedication to the awakening of all beings.

o: a debt you carry for past wrongdoing
a blessing that only a monk can give you
the goodness that comes from good actions

games.q: match the piece of sharing the merit.
p: merit, the good from good actions
well done: rejoicing in another's good

s: sharing merit means you lose some of it
teachers compare it to lighting one candle from another: the room just gets brighter.
an old text pictures dead relatives waiting outside the walls of their home
the discourse outside the walls; the living dedicate their gifts to them.
Mahayana traditions dedicate it to the awakening of all beings.

games.q: you've just finished a morning sitting and feel a little calmer. what do many Buddhists do next?
o: keep the calm for yourself: you earned it.
dedicate the good of the sitting to others.
start the next task right away.
games.why: practice traditionally ends with a dedication: whatever good was done is shared, with relatives, with all beings.

practice: Bring to mind whatever good came from this practice, a little calm, a little kindness, a little clarity, and picture it as water in a small cup.

Pour it out in a thin, steady stream, flowing on to someone you love, someone you've lost, a stranger, all beings. If you'd like, use the old words, idam vo natinam hotu, may this be for our relatives; or simply open your hands.

wordCard.voice: Punna. Merit, the goodness from good actions: shared at the end of practice, like water poured out until it reaches the sea.

carryVoice: Your line: may it be shared. The good doesn't stop at you. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 7 / Petavatthu 1.5 (Tirokudda Sutta), 'idam vo natinam hotu'
